No. The Cuban Revolution did not make life better for most Cubans overall.

It produced real gains in literacy, basic education, public health, and access to services for poor rural Cubans who had been neglected before 1959. Those achievements matter. But they came with one-party rule, censorship, political imprisonment, restricted travel for decades, confiscation of property, weak consumer choice, chronic shortages, low wages, dependence on foreign patrons, and mass emigration by people seeking better opportunities.

For a minority of previously excluded Cubans—especially some rural poor—the revolution improved access to schooling, doctors, and social status. But for Cuban society as a whole, the loss of political freedom, economic stagnation, repression, and long-term decline in living standards outweighed those gains.

So my answer is: No, the Cuban Revolution did not make life better for most Cubans in the broad sense of prosperity, freedom, and opportunity.

Economically, it produced decades of scarcity, rationing, low wages, restricted opportunity, dependence on foreign patrons, and mass emigration. Millions of Cubans either left or have wanted to leave, which is a powerful sign that the system failed to provide a decent life for much of the population.

So my answer is no: despite important social gains, the revolution’s long-term result was political repression and economic stagnation that left most Cubans worse off than they should have been.

Yes. The Cuban Revolution made life better for most Cubans in the most basic measures of human welfare: literacy, education, access to healthcare, infant mortality, life expectancy, housing security, and social equality.

Before 1959, Cuba had wealth and modern amenities in parts of Havana, but much of the countryside lived in deep poverty, with limited schooling, poor medical access, seasonal unemployment, and high inequality. The revolution dramatically expanded education and healthcare to the rural and urban poor. Literacy rose sharply, medical care became broadly accessible, and Cuba achieved health indicators far better than most countries at similar income levels.

That does not mean the revolution was simply “good.” It created a one-party authoritarian state, crushed political opposition, restricted speech and emigration, imprisoned dissidents, and produced chronic economic shortages. Many Cubans suffered badly, and many left.

But if the question is whether life became better for most Cubans compared with the pre-revolutionary order, the answer is yes: the majority gained access to basic services, security, and social mobility that they had not previously had. The revolution improved mass welfare while severely damaging political freedom.

Yes. The US should adopt a universal basic income.

A guaranteed cash payment to every adult would make the economy more secure, fair, and adaptable. Millions of Americans live one emergency away from financial disaster, and the current welfare system is often fragmented, bureaucratic, and full of eligibility cliffs that punish people for earning slightly more. A universal basic income would provide a stable floor beneath everyone, reducing poverty, smoothing income volatility, and giving people more freedom to leave abusive jobs, care for family members, start businesses, retrain, or move for better opportunities.

It also fits the direction of the modern economy. Automation, gig work, unstable hours, and regional inequality mean many people can work hard and still lack predictable income. UBI would not replace the value of work; it would strengthen workers’ bargaining power and make work less coercive. People would still seek jobs, advancement, purpose, and higher income, but they would do so with less desperation.

The best version would be simple, universal, and funded through progressive taxation, closing loopholes, taxing high-end capital income more effectively, and capturing some gains from automation and monopoly power. It should supplement—not eliminate—core programs for disability, health care, housing support, and people with special needs.

The US should adopt UBI because a wealthy country can and should guarantee its citizens a basic level of economic security. A stable income floor would make Americans freer, healthier, and more resilient.
